background.definition: Otosclerosis is a disorder of bone metabolism in the middle ear, most frequently involving the stapediovestibular joint, which leads to slowly progressive conductive hearing loss. Symptoms usually occur between the ages of 15 years and 45 years, and most often begin in the patient's early 20s. Otosclerosis is bilateral in 70% to 80% of patients.

list.listitem: The lifetime incidence is 10% for histologic disease and 1% for clinically significant disease in whites in the United States.
The prevalence is 0.3% to 0.04% (range = 0.2%-2.0%).
The incidence in whites is twice the incidence in Asians and 10 times the incidence in blacks.
Otosclerosis causes 5% to 9% of all hearing loss and 18% to 22% of conductive hearing loss.
Genetic: 50% to 70% of patients have a positive family history. If both parents have otosclerosis, the risk for a child is 50%.
Otosclerosis is thought to be autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.
Viral etiology has been proposed and measles has been implicated.
A hormonal influence is suggested with female predominance and occurrence during child-bearing years. Otosclerosis may worsen during pregnancy.
There is localized disorder of bone metabolism in the otic capsule.
There is disordered resorption and deposition of bone in the middle ear (primarily the stapes). The abnormal bone fixates the stapes in the oval window, thus interfering with sound conduction.
Lesions occasionally (8%) affect the inner ear resulting in sensorineural hearing loss.
The value of routine screening for hearing loss to improve patient outcomes has not been evaluated in a randomized clinical trial. B
No specific otosclerosis screening guidelines exist, although some experts recommend impedance-audiometry screening in children at high risk (ie, those with a positive family history). C

CT scanning is an accurate confirmatory test with a sensitivity of 80% to 85%. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History of otitis and abnormal ear examination result are present
Severe vestibular symptoms and tinnitus are usually present
Systemic symptoms and pain will be present
Blue sclera and other bony abnormalities are present
Usually present in the first decade of life

list.listitem: Patients typically present with gradually progressive hearing loss, usually to low tones and whispers. Otosclerosis is bilateral in 70% of patients. It is also more common in women and in whites.
Vestibular symptoms are unusual (<25%), but tinnitus is common (75%).
The physical examination is usually normal. Ten percent of patients may show a Schwartze's sign, which is a reddish-blue discoloration behind the tympanic membrane.
Tuning fork examination may indicate a conductive hearing loss.

The audiogram normally shows a slowly worsening conductive hearing loss progressing from low to high frequencies. If the cochlea is involved, a mixed sensorineural/conductive hearing loss will be seen.
Tympanometry: type A "stiffness" response is found
CT scan is an accurate tool (sensitivity = 80%-85%) to show abnormal bone deposition in the temporal bone and to assist in the diagnosis of otosclerosis.
Otosclerosis should be suspected in a patient between the ages of 15 years and 45 years who presents with gradual onset of hearing loss. A positive family history makes the diagnosis more likely.
Audiologic evaluation is necessary to determine the extent and type of hearing deficit.
High-dose sodium fluoride (20-40 mg per day) has been shown to stabilize hearing loss in 50% of patients and lead to improvement in 30% of patients. B
Surgical treatment provides excellent outcomes, with 90%-95% of patients having significant audiologic improvement. A

High-dose sodium fluoride (20-40 mg per day) has been shown to stabilize hearing loss in 50% of patients and lead to improvement in 30% of patients. It may be most effective in those with sensorineural loss, but its overall efficacy is uncertain.

Bisphosphonates have been suggested as a possible treatment. One prospective double-blinded study was performed and although statistically significant improvements were not shown there was a trend toward stabilization and improvement in some hearing frequencies. One uncontrolled study showed improvement of neuro-otologic symptoms.
Indications for surgical management include a conductive hearing loss with a greater than 20 dB air-bone gap.
The goal is to release the stapes fixation and allow transmission of sound along the ossicles and into the oval window.

Approaches to surgical management include total stapedectomy, partial stapedectomy, and stapedotomy. Significant clinical improvement occurs in 90% to 95% of patients. Two percent might experience additional hearing loss.
Pediatric stapedotomy can be effective and safe based on an observational trial.
Although there are no RCT results comparing stapedectomy with stapedotomy, results appear to be similar.
A variety of prostheses are used. Usually these are autograft tissues from a hand vein, perichondrium of the ear, or temporalis fascia.
No statistically significant difference in hearing thresholds at 3 months could be demonstrated between the different prosthesis types.
More studies are needed on a possible role for cochlear implants.
Hearing aids can help patients with mild disease and those who are not candidates for surgery. However, since most patients are young, surgery is the preferred option.

The prognosis is very good with surgical treatment and up to 90% to 95% of patients experience elimination of conductive hearing loss. The rate of deterioration with time does not exceed that due to presbycusis. B
Long-term follow-up showed beneficial results maintained up to 30 years in 75% of patients. B
